 Fear of Harsh Winter Gas Outages Sparks Rush for Gas Cylinders and Massive Price Hikes in Iran
 November 16, 2026 
 5 min read
 Concerns over pressure drops and gas outages have fueled a booming market for buying and selling gas cylinders. 
 One seller has listed an empty, secondhand, rusted cylinder on Divar for 7 million tomans, while another has priced a similar but slightly cleaner cylinder at 8 million tomans. Prices for brand-new, empty cylinders typically start at 9 million tomans, while pre-filled ones sell for 10 million tomans. 
 "Have you bought a gas cylinder yet? If not, definitely think about buying at least two; they say we’re going to have a harsh winter this year." This sentence has become the talk of the town among many families these days. Perhaps until a week or two ago, such conversations were mostly heard among residents of the eastern provinces, from Golestan to Razavi Khorasan. Yet the situation appears to be far worse than those rumors, with talk of pressure drops and gas outages now reaching Tehran as well.
 Fatemeh, who has a three-year-old daughter and lives in Bojnord, says: "For the past month or two, whispers that the gas situation might become critical this winter and cause outages in our city stirred up panic among people. Many went looking in their storage rooms for old gas cylinders and portable camping stoves, but because most were empty, we had to find somewhere to fill them and store them for winter." However, since these items have been obsolete for years and few people use them anymore, the number of gas-refilling stations has dwindled significantly.
 After asking around extensively, Fatemeh’s husband found a station in the lower part of town, only to be met with a long line when they went to refill Fatemeh’s grandmother’s old cylinder: "It seemed like many others, just like us, had thought of using gas cylinders and camping stoves for the winter. That was a month ago. Back then, the cost of filling an 11-kilogram gas cylinder, the kind used in kitchens in the old days, was 400,000 tomans. Because the line was so long, we gave up on filling it that day and decided to go early the following Thursday morning. When we returned the next week,the refilling cost had jumped to 600,000 tomans."
 According to Fatemeh, the closer winter gets and the higher the public demand for filling and stockpiling gas cylinders climbs, the steeper the costs become: "My sister lives in Mashhad. A few days ago, she managed to buy two empty cylinders on the Divar classifieds app, and when she went to get them filled, the cost had reached one million tomans."
 Scrolling through listings on Divar these days reveals a surge of buyers and sellers trading all types of full and empty, new and secondhand gas cylinders and camping stoves at wildly varying prices, with everyone selling for whatever they can get. Meanwhile, numerous vendors have jumped into the fray with competitive sales ads.
 One seller has listed an empty, secondhand, rusted cylinder on Divar for 7 million tomans, while another is asking 8 million tomans for a similar but slightly cleaner one. Prices for brand-new empty cylinders typically start at 9 million tomans, while pre-filled ones go for 10 million tomans. Naturally, these prices continue to climb as winter approaches.This stands in stark contrast to just a few months ago, when no one gave such things a second thought and you could barely find a gas cylinder on Divar - and even then, for at most 2 million tomans.
 A shop around Tehran’s Shoush Street has taped a sign to its storefront window reading: "Don’t overpay for gas cylinders - be sure to get a quote from us first." Inside the shop, the vendor explains: "We are manufacturers ourselves; our factory is right here in Pakdasht, which is why our prices are reasonable. As for safety standards, don’t worry at all - the official standard seal is stamped on every cylinder."
 A 50-kilogram cylinder sells for 18 million tomans, a 25-kilogram for 14 million, an 11-kilogram for 8 million, and a portable camping cylinder for 2 million tomans. Refilling isn't a problem either, he says: "I’ll refer you to a place that fills cylinders at a fair price, below market rates. Filling an 11-kilogram cylinder costs one million tomans, and a 50-kilogram cylinder costs 5 million."
 "In my opinion, the 50-kilogram one is the most economical," the vendor adds. "At least you’ll get through this winter with peace of mind, without worrying about your wife and kids freezing or how to cook."
 The specter of returning to the past - standing in long lines to refill gas cylinders or chasing delivery trucks down alleys and streets, all under the pressure and threat of a war that could reignite any day - has deeply rattled the public. With little hope for improvement or decisive action from authorities, people have taken matters into their own hands to survive the coming winter however they can.
 Arman, an engineer working at the South Pars complex in Asaluyeh, describes the country’s gas production situation as far bleaker than what officials have disclosed to the public. Speaking to IranWire, he says: "Since the 40-day war,conditions have never returned to normal. Large sections of the facilities remain shut down, work shifts are shorter,working days have been reduced, and output at this facility and other power plants across the country has dropped sharply because sufficient fuel is not reaching the plants."
 According to him, to manage the shortfall, household gas pressure in the southern provinces has been reduced since the start of autumn. Industries are faring even worse, with many manufacturing plants forced into early winter hibernation:"There are whispers about shifting part of the gas consumption burden onto electricity, but the situation at electric power plants is dire too. Without fuel reaching the power plants, how are they supposed to generate extra electricity? They are already barely scraping by to manage power consumption. Rest assured, if things continue like this, we will face an electricity imbalance crisis this winter as well."
 The looming threat of gas shortages and outages doesn't seem to worry ordinary citizens alone; government officials are anxious too, though their concern centers on rising public discontent and street protests.
 The Iranian Students Polling Agency (ISPA) recently conducted a public opinion survey on energy imbalances. According to the poll’s findings, published in June of this year, while energy had not yet become the public’s number-one daily concern, it carries immense potential to escalate into a major social issue with serious repercussions.
